title: App maintenance cost in India: a yearly budget
description: App maintenance in India costs 15 to 25% of the build a year. Store deadlines, hosting, API price changes, AMC contracts and a yearly budget template.

contentHtml:
What app maintenance costs per year in India

In short: Most published estimates put yearly app maintenance at 15 to 25 percent of what the app cost to build. On a ₹10 lakh app, plan for roughly ₹1.5 lakh to ₹2.5 lakh a year in developer time, plus hosting, Apple's 99 USD yearly fee and whatever your third-party services charge. Some of that work is forced on you: Google Play and Apple both set deadlines your app has to meet to stay listed.

Owners usually budget carefully for the build and then treat year two as free. It is not. The phone your customer bought last month runs a newer operating system than the one your app was tested on, and the stores will not wait for you to catch up.

If you want the build and the first year of upkeep written down before you commit, that is part of what our ₹3,500 requirement analysis produces: a call with the people who would build it, the requirements worked through, and a written fixed quotation and timeline (how it works). Everything below works without us.

This guide was checked in November 2026, against Google Play's target API page and Apple's upcoming requirements page as they stood on 16 November 2026. Both change every year, so check them again before you sign next year's budget.

What published estimates say

There is no official figure for maintenance. What exists is a handful of estimates from development firms, and they agree more than I expected.

Published yearly maintenance estimates, as a share of the original build cost

SourceYearly maintenanceWhat they say it covers
SolGuruz (India)15 to 25% of initial development costUpdates, bug fixes, OS compatibility patches, new feature releases; its FAQ adds server costs and API subscriptions
Zartek (India)15 to 20% of the original budgetKeeping the app working through OS updates
Vrinsofts15 to 20% of the original budgetHosting, monitoring, bug fixes, security updates, performance work, support

Source: SolGuruz and Zartek and Vrinsofts, read 16 November 2026.

Two things stand out. First, the floor is consistent: nobody I read suggests less than 15 percent. Second, the sources do not agree on what the percentage includes. SolGuruz's FAQ folds server costs and API subscriptions into its 15 to 25 percent. Vrinsofts breaks hosting and monitoring out as separate monthly lines. So when a vendor quotes you a maintenance percentage, ask what is inside it before you compare it with anyone else's.

Vrinsofts also says the first year after launch is often the most expensive, because that is when real users find the bugs, and gives monthly ranges in US dollars: hosting from $70 to $500 or more, monitoring tools from $50 to $500, and total maintenance between $500 and $4,000 a month for most businesses. Those are global agency numbers, not Indian freelancer rates, so treat them as an upper reference rather than a target.

For where the build cost itself comes from, our breakdown of mobile app development cost in India covers published ranges and hourly rates.

What maintenance actually covers

Here is the list I would use, in roughly the order it bites. The first two are not optional: they come from the stores, with dates.

Android: Google Play's target API deadline

Every Android app declares a target API level, which tells the phone which version of Android it was built for. Google Play raises the minimum every year. According to Google Play's target API page, starting 31 August 2026 new apps and app updates must target Android 16 (API level 36) or higher to be submitted.

Existing apps that do nothing are not removed, but they shrink. Apps must target Android 15 (API level 35) or higher to stay available to new users on newer phones. An app that targets Android 14 or lower is shown only to people whose phones run that version or older. Google's page says people who already installed it are not affected, but new customers on new phones cannot find or download it.

Google offered an extension to 1 November 2026 for developers who asked through Play Console. That date has passed as I write this, so if your app still targets API level 34 or lower, it is already invisible to new users on current phones.

Moving up a level is not a setting you flip. The Android migration guide lists behaviour changes for each version, and each one can touch permissions, notifications, background work or storage. Your third-party SDKs (payments, analytics, maps) also have to support the new level. This is real developer time, every year.

iPhone: Apple's SDK and Xcode requirements

Apple works the same way with a different lever. Its upcoming requirements page says that since 28 April 2026, apps uploaded to App Store Connect must be built with Xcode 26 or later, using the iOS 26 SDK. Since 9 September 2026, iOS and iPadOS apps uploaded must target iOS 13 or later.

The practical effect: you cannot ship even a one-line bug fix to an iPhone app that was last built with an older toolchain until someone rebuilds it with the current one. If the app has not been touched for a year or two, that rebuild is when old libraries break. The page has dated entries going back years, including an age rating update all apps had to respond to by 31 January 2026, so expect at least one Apple change a year.

Hosting and backend

Your app talks to a server: a database, a login system, file storage, perhaps an admin panel. That runs on a cloud bill that grows with users. Many small apps start on Firebase, whose pricing page offers a no-cost Spark plan with usage limits and a pay-as-you-go Blaze plan that keeps the Spark no-cost usage and bills above it. Other stacks run on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud with similar pay-for-what-you-use billing.

Hosting is the line that surprises people in good years, because more customers means more reads, more storage and more bandwidth. Ask your developer for last month's bill and the main thing driving it.

Monitoring and crash reports

Someone has to notice when the app breaks. Crash reporting, uptime checks and error logs are cheap or free at small scale, but someone still has to read them. Vrinsofts lists monitoring tools at $50 to $500 a month for the bigger setups. The bigger cost is the hour a week a developer spends looking. We go into this in observability before you need it.

Security patches

Libraries your app depends on publish security fixes, and the operating systems change their permission rules. Google's target API page says each new Android version brings security, privacy and performance improvements, and some of them only apply once your app targets that version. Keeping dependencies current is the unglamorous part of maintenance that prevents the expensive part. Our security basics for startups lists what to check first.

Store fees

These are the only fixed numbers in this post. Apple's enrolment page says the Apple Developer Program costs 99 USD a year, in local currency where available, and that enrolment in India is only available through the Apple Developer app. Google Play has a US$25 one-time registration fee. So iPhone costs you every year; Android costs you once.

Third-party API price changes

This is the line nobody budgets for, because the price is set by someone else and can move under you. Two recent examples.

Google Maps. On 1 March 2025, Google replaced its 200 USD monthly credit with free monthly usage per service. Its own India example: an India-based customer making 90,000 Geocoding (India) requests a month paid $0 under the old credit, and from March 2025 gets 70,000 free requests and pays $30 a month for the rest. Another India example in the same page went the other way, from $241 a month to $0. Same app, different bill, because the rules changed.

WhatsApp. Meta replaced conversation-based pricing with per-message pricing on 1 July 2025, and its pricing page says rates may change on the first day of each quarter. If your app sends order updates or OTPs on WhatsApp, that line can change four times a year.

The same applies to SMS, payment gateways, AI APIs and anything else billed per use. The defence is a list of every paid service the app calls, with its current rate and the page where the provider publishes changes.

AMC contracts in India

In India, ongoing upkeep is usually sold as an AMC, an annual maintenance contract: a fixed yearly fee for a defined set of support work. The term comes from hardware and has carried over to software.

What an AMC includes varies a lot. As one example, Mobisoft Infotech's software AMC page lists security patches, routine upgrades, performance work, support for third-party integrations and APIs, monthly performance reports and incident logs, and a support SLA with response and resolution times set by issue severity. That is a fuller contract than many small apps get.

Before you sign one, I would get answers to these in writing:

  • Is the yearly Android target API update included? It is the one piece of work you know will be needed every year.
  • Is the Apple Xcode rebuild included? Same reason.
  • How many developer hours a month does the fee cover, and what is the rate beyond them?
  • What are the response times, by severity, and do they apply on weekends?
  • Are hosting and third-party bills inside the fee or passed through? Passed through at cost is easier to check.
  • What counts as a new feature and is therefore outside the AMC?
  • Whose name are the cloud, store and code accounts in? They should be yours, so you can change vendors without a rebuild.

That last point matters more than any rate. At ElevateBox, code, cloud and credentials stay in the client's name, and I would ask the same of any vendor.

How to build your yearly budget, step by step

Here is how I would put the number together for a small business app, starting from what you already know.

Step 1. Write down the build cost. Use the total you paid for the first version, including design and backend, not only the app screens. This is the base for the percentage.

Step 2. Apply the labour range. Multiply by 15 percent for a low estimate and 25 percent for a high one. That is the developer time for updates, fixes and compatibility work.

Step 3. Add the store fees. Apple's 99 USD a year if you are on iPhone. Google Play's US$25 is already paid if you are live.

Step 4. List every paid service. Hosting, database, SMS, WhatsApp, maps, payments, email, crash reporting, AI. For each, write the current monthly cost and where the provider publishes price changes.

Step 5. Mark the dated work. Put Google Play's August deadline and Apple's spring SDK change in the calendar, and ask your developer for an estimate for each.

Step 6. Add a buffer. I would hold back 10 percent of the total for a price change or a library that breaks. Then review the budget every quarter against the real bills.

A yearly budget template

Copy this into a spreadsheet. Fill the right-hand column with your own numbers; the middle column tells you where each one comes from.

Yearly app maintenance budget template

LineHow to estimate itYour figure (₹)
Developer time: updates and fixes15 to 25% of build cost
Android target API updateDeveloper estimate, before August
iPhone SDK and Xcode rebuildDeveloper estimate, before Apple's spring deadline
Apple Developer Program99 USD a year in local currency
Google Play registrationUS$25 once; nothing if already paid
Hosting and databaseLast 3 months of bills, times 4, plus growth
Monitoring and crash reportingTool bill plus review time
SMS, WhatsApp, maps, paymentsPer-use rate times expected volume
Security and dependency updatesUsually inside developer time; check
Buffer for price changesAbout 10% of the total

Source: Apple Developer and Google Play Console Help and SolGuruz, read 16 November 2026.

Three worked examples

The businesses and build costs below are illustrative, chosen to show how the arithmetic works. They are not quotes.

A clinic booking app

Say a two-doctor clinic paid ₹6 lakh for a booking app on Android and iPhone, with a small admin panel for the receptionist (illustrative).

Developer time at 15 to 25 percent: ₹90,000 to ₹1,50,000 a year. Apple: 99 USD. Hosting for a few hundred patients a month may fit inside a free tier such as Firebase's Spark plan, but check the bill rather than assume. SMS or WhatsApp reminders are the per-use line to watch.

What this tells you: for a small clinic, the yearly cost is mostly developer time, and most of that is the two store deadlines. If the AMC does not name them, it is not covering the work you know is coming. Clinics that want online booking without an app at all can start smaller; see appointment systems.

A D2C brand's shopping app

Say a clothing brand paid ₹15 lakh for a shopping app with payments, order tracking and push notifications (illustrative).

Developer time: ₹2,25,000 to ₹3,75,000 a year. Hosting grows with sale days. The payment gateway, WhatsApp order updates and any maps or address lookup are all per use, and each provider can change its price.

What this tells you: a shopping app has the most third-party lines, so Step 4 matters most here. A Google Maps style change that moves you from free to paid at your volume is a real monthly bill. Ask for a list of every SDK in the app with its pricing page.

A coaching institute's student app

Say a coaching institute paid ₹8 lakh for a student app with video lessons, tests and OTP login (illustrative).

Developer time: ₹1,20,000 to ₹2,00,000 a year. Video storage and streaming will likely be the biggest hosting cost, and it rises with every batch. OTP login means an SMS or WhatsApp bill that grows with admissions.

What this tells you: plan hosting around the academic calendar, because usage peaks before exams. If the institute also sends batch updates on WhatsApp, that is another per-message line to add in Step 4.

Five ways maintenance budgets mislead you

Treating the percentage as all-in. SolGuruz puts servers and APIs inside its range; Vrinsofts lists them separately. Two quotes at 20 percent can cover very different things.

Budgeting for year two as if it were year five. Vrinsofts says the first year after launch is often the most expensive. Real users find bugs that testers did not.

Skipping a year of updates. Each skipped Android or Apple change makes the next one bigger, because the jumps stack. An app untouched for two years can need weeks of work just to upload a fix.

Ignoring prices you do not set. Google Maps and WhatsApp both changed how they bill in 2025. Your budget is only as stable as your least stable provider.

Paying for maintenance with no list of what was done. Ask for a monthly note: what was updated, what was fixed, what is due next. If an update gets rejected by a store, our post on app store rejections covers the usual reasons.

A quarterly maintenance check

Once a quarter, sit with your developer for half an hour and go through this.

A 30-minute quarterly app maintenance check

MinutesWhat to checkWhat you write down
First 10Google Play Console and App Store Connect for warnings and policy noticesAny deadline and the estimate to meet it
Next 10Hosting and every per-use bill against last quarterLines that grew, and why
Next 5Crash reports and reviews mentioning bugsTop three fixes for next quarter
Last 5Provider pricing pages for maps, messaging and paymentsAny announced change and its effect

After a year of this, you will know your real maintenance number, and next year's budget stops being a guess.

Frequently asked questions

No. Google Play has a US$25 one-time registration fee. Apple's Developer Program is 99 USD every year, in local currency where available.
